kurz: How a loan is broken down into tradable units, what face value, coupon, accrued interest and ranking mean, and what distinguishes a bond from owning shares.

bloecke.md:
When you buy a bond, you buy a piece of a loan. The issuer, for example a government, a bank or a company, needs money and, instead of borrowing it from a single bank, borrows it from many thousands of creditors at the same time. To do so, it divides the debt into standardised units with identical terms. This creates a security that can be resold on the stock exchange without the debtor having to agree. This tradability is what distinguishes a bond from an ordinary loan.

The bond market is larger than the stock market. According to figures from the US industry association SIFMA, bonds worth $160.7 trillion were outstanding worldwide at the end of 2025, while the market value of all shares together came to $157.8 trillion. The Federal Republic of Germany alone, according to its Finance Agency (Finanzagentur), always has around 80 highly liquid securities outstanding, which together form an almost gapless yield curve.

## Five details that describe a bond

The **issuer** is the debtor. Whether the promise to pay is worth anything at all depends on the issuer. In 2026, the Federal Republic of Germany is rated in the highest category by all six rating agencies listed by the Finance Agency (Moody's, S&P, Fitch, Scope, DBRS and KBRA). A medium-sized issuer is usually far from that. How creditworthiness, that is the issuer's ability to pay its debts, is reflected in prices is the subject of a later lesson.

The **face value** is the amount repaid at the end. It is the bond's unit of account, not its price. German federal securities have a denomination of €0.01 and can therefore be divided down to the cent. For corporate bonds the minimum denomination is often considerably larger, so some of these securities are practically out of the question for small portfolios.

The **coupon** is the annual interest as a percentage of the face value. It is fixed at issue and does not change afterwards. Floating rates and inflation linking also exist, but they are the exception and are covered later.

The **term** fixes the day on which the face value is repaid. After that the security no longer exists. This is where the structure of a bond differs most clearly from that of a share, because a bond has a fixed end date from the start.

The **ranking** states where the creditor stands if the issuer can no longer pay. It is laid down in the bond's terms and conditions and is the detail there that is most often overlooked.

The coupon always refers to the face value and never to the purchase price. A bond with a 2.5% coupon pays €2.50 per €100 of face value, regardless of whether you bought it at 91.53 or at 112. How much the buyer earns from it is shown by a different figure: the yield.

bloecke.titel: Cash flows per €100 of face value
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a 2.5% coupon and a ten-year term. Ten coupons of €2.50 are followed by repayment of the face value, which accounts for most of the payments.

bloecke.md:
## Price quotation as a percentage

Bond prices are quoted as a percentage of face value, not in euros per unit. “Price 91.53” means €91.53 per €100 of face value. This convention exists because bonds are traded with completely different nominal amounts and denominations. Only the percentage quotation makes the prices of two securities directly comparable.

A price of exactly 100 is called *par*. A security whose fixed coupon is above the current market interest rate trades above par; one whose coupon is too low trades below par. The model bond from above, with a ten-year term and a 2.5% coupon, has a calculated price of 91.53 at the Bund yield of 3.52% on 18 September 2026. How this price comes about and how the yield to maturity follows from it is covered in the next lesson. For the structure of the bond, it is enough here that the coupon and face value are fixed and the price fluctuates.

## Interest entitlement between two coupon dates

A bond pays its coupon on a fixed day each year. A buyer who purchases it four weeks before this date would receive the full annual payment on the coupon date, even though they have only provided their money for four weeks. Conversely, the seller would have lost the interest entitlement for eleven months without compensation.

This is balanced out by **accrued interest**. It is the portion of interest that has built up since the last coupon date but has not yet been paid out. The buyer reimburses it to the seller in addition to the price. The interest entitlement thus changes hands together with the security, without the issuer being involved.

bloecke.formel: Accrued interest = Coupon × Days since last payment / Days in interest period
bloecke.erklaerung: The annual coupon is split between seller and buyer to the exact day. How the days are counted is set by the day count convention in the bond's terms and conditions. For all coupon-paying German federal securities this is act/act according to ICMA. Here the number of calendar days is divided by the length of the interest period in calendar days.

bloecke.beispiel: With €10,000 face value, a 2.5% coupon and 35 days since the coupon date, the result is 250 × 35 / 365 = €23.97.

bloecke.titel: Example of a purchase contract note
bloecke.md:
Model bond with a 2.5% coupon, coupon date 18 August and ten years' remaining maturity. Purchase on Friday 18 September 2026 of €10,000 face value at a price of 91.53. Delivery and payment take place two business days later on Tuesday 22 September (value date). Accrued interest runs from the last coupon date to the day before the value date.

- Market value: 10,000 × 91.53 / 100 = €9,153.00
- Accrued interest for 35 days: 250 × 35 / 365 = €23.97
- Settlement amount excluding fees: €9,176.97

On 18 August of the following year the issuer transfers the full €250, regardless of who held the security and for how long. Of this, €23.97 is merely the repayment of the amount the buyer advanced at purchase. The buyer's interest income for the first period is €226.03 and corresponds to the 330 days for which they held the security.

bloecke.titel: Clean price and dirty price over two years
bloecke.unter: Schematic illustration with the price held constant for clarity. The amount payable rises daily by the accrued interest and drops back abruptly on the coupon date, which is why charts show the clean price.

bloecke.md: Price lists and charts show the clean price so that the price line does not jump in a sawtooth pattern by the coupon amount every year. What you pay is the dirty price, that is the price including accrued interest. When you buy a security with a high coupon shortly before the interest date, this can quickly add several per cent of the face value to the market value. That is not a loss, but it is a cash requirement that the order screen does not show beforehand. Accrued interest is treated separately for tax purposes. The details are in the tax module.

The day count convention determines how days are counted. It is part of the contract.

Under **act/act (ICMA)**, the calendar days are counted and divided by the length of the interest period in calendar days. All coupon-paying German federal securities are calculated this way.

The **30/360** method assumes months of 30 days and years of 360 days. From 18 August to 22 September it counts 34 days instead of 35. Many corporate bonds and the entire traditional US corporate bond market use this method.

Under **act/360**, the calendar days are also counted, but divided by 360. Bubills, the federal government's non-interest-bearing money market securities, are discounted this way. No accrued interest arises on them because they have no coupon.

In the example, an annual coupon of €250 produces €23.97 of accrued interest under act/act, but only €23.61 under 30/360. On €10,000 of face value that is a difference of 36 cents; on a trading position of €50 million it is around €1,800 per transaction.

## Bondholder and shareholder

The shareholder buys a stake in the company. They own a fraction of what remains after all debts have been deducted. This claim has no upper limit, but it is not promised either. The bondholder, by contrast, buys a debt claim. They own nothing of the company, but they have an enforceable right to fixed amounts on fixed dates.

All other differences follow from this one. If the issuer increases its profit fivefold, the bondholder still receives only the coupon. If, on the other hand, a payment is not made, the issuer is in default, and that has legal consequences. The best case for the bondholder is therefore that all payments are made as agreed. The return is capped by contract on the upside and open on the downside, all the way to a total loss. Because of this asymmetry, bond analysis is above all risk analysis, and equity analysis above all opportunity analysis.

bloecke.md:
## Order of ranking in insolvency

The statement “bonds rank ahead of shares” is correct but too crude. The Insolvency Code (InsO) sets out an order with several levels. Secured creditors are satisfied in advance from their collateral. From the remaining insolvency estate, each level is served only once the level above has been satisfied in full. Partial satisfaction of the higher level is not enough.

Secured creditors have a right to separate satisfaction (Absonderungsrecht) from certain assets (Sections 49 to 51 InsO) and are paid in advance from their realisation. If the insolvency administrator realises a movable item or a receivable, a flat 4% for assessment costs and 5% for realisation costs go from the proceeds to the estate (Sections 170, 171 InsO); the secured creditor receives the rest up to the amount of its claim. If the proceeds are not sufficient, the creditor takes part with the shortfall as an ordinary insolvency creditor (Section 52 InsO). From the remaining estate, the costs of the proceedings and the liabilities of the estate are paid first (Sections 53 to 55 InsO), because without them no proceedings would take place. Only then comes the large group of ordinary insolvency creditors under Section 38 InsO. These include suppliers, employees with claims from before the proceedings and holders of normal, unsecured bonds. They share what is left pro rata, that is in proportion to their claims.

Below them are the subordinated claims under Section 39 InsO. These include interest that accrues only after the proceedings have been opened, fines, claims arising from gratuitous benefits provided by the debtor, and shareholder loans. Subordinated bonds are placed in this level by contract, and their higher coupon is the payment for this. Equity no longer appears in the statutory list. It appears only in Section 199 InsO, which governs what happens to a surplus if all insolvency creditors could be satisfied in full. Shareholders therefore do not form a ranking level of their own. They receive only what is left over after that.

bloecke.titel: Order of ranking in insolvency proceedings
bloecke.unter: The levels are ordered from top to bottom. Secured creditors are satisfied in advance from their collateral; from the remaining estate, each level is served only once the level above has been satisfied in full.

bloecke.md: In the German insolvency proceedings opened in 2011 and concluded by the end of 2018, creditors recovered an average of 3.8% of their claims. They had to forgo 96.2% (Federal Statistical Office). The figure covers all proceedings, including the many small insolvencies without assets. It is therefore unsuitable as an estimate of the recovery rate for a listed corporate bond. The tendency holds nonetheless, because when there are hardly any assets, even a good ranking is of little use. Priority over equity only establishes an order; it does not guarantee repayment.

bloecke.titel: Credit risk and interest rate risk
bloecke.md: Credit risk and interest rate risk are two separate risks. A security can be free of one and fully exposed to the other. Credit risk is about whether the issuer pays in the end. Interest rate risk is about what the security is worth today if you have to sell it before maturity. A German federal bond has practically no credit risk and still lost a double-digit percentage of its market value in 2022, when the yield on ten-year Bunds rose by 274 basis points. Nor can a bond be equated with an interest-bearing account, because there is no deposit protection for securities in a securities account.

mitnehmen: A bond is a loan broken down into tradable units, with a fixed coupon on the face value and a fixed repayment date, which gives no stake in the company.
The coupon refers to the face value, and the price is quoted as a percentage of face value, but neither figure on its own says anything about the return.

Accrued interest is the interest income due to the seller for the time since the last coupon date; the buyer pays it in addition to the market value and gets it back with the next coupon, which is why the settlement amount is higher than the market value.
In insolvency, the bondholder ranks ahead of the owner but behind the costs of the proceedings and the secured creditors, and subordinated bonds rank even further back, behind normal bonds.
Credit risk and interest rate risk are different risks, and a security without one can be heavily exposed to the other.

begriffe.text: The amount in which a bond is denominated and which is repaid at maturity. It is the reference value for the coupon and for the percentage quotation of the price, but not the price of the security.
The annual interest set at issue as a percentage of the face value. It does not change during the term and is independent of the price at which an investor bought.

The portion of interest that has built up since the last coupon date and has not yet been paid out. The buyer reimburses it to the seller in addition to the price. For the seller it is interest income; for the buyer it is an advance that is recovered with the next coupon.

The quoted price excluding accrued interest. Charts and price lists show it so that the price history does not jump by the coupon amount every year. The amount payable on purchase including accrued interest is called the dirty price.
A price of exactly 100% of the face value. A security with a coupon that is high compared with the market interest rate trades above par; one with a coupon that is too low trades below par.
A bond that, by contract, ranks behind all ordinary insolvency creditors in the event of insolvency (ranking under Section 39 InsO). The higher coupon is the compensation for this weaker position.
